title: Contracts limited the itinerary; warm receptions and comparison with Armstrong
summary: Contract arrangements kept them from more countries, but Swedish and Danish welcomes, honorary club memberships and London concerts followed, and some thought his band better than Armstrong's.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: The airport. Well, what it was, we had a chance to go to all those places, to Italy, France, Vienna, all those places we had a chance to go to after we got there. But trouble was, when they signed the contracts, they had made an arrangement for George to play three weeks with Kaye in Germany, you see. And after we got there, everybody wanted to book the band in these different places, you see. They wanted the band to play in Holland, Vienna, Italy, France, Austria, and Belgium. But by having them three weeks, George had to be there about a month before we could even went on this tour, you see. And then the fellows wasn't going to stay and pay the expense three or four weeks before they could go away. But everywhere that we played at, they actually was asked to return. And when we got to Sweden, they had three little young kids. One was 16, one was 17, and one was 21. And it was cold and ice on the ground and everything. And those kids were out there with just a banjo, a clarinet, and a soprano. And they was out there playing Dixieland, Welcome the Band to Sweden. Yeah. And those things really was touching. And we played another place in Denmark. I can't think of the name of the town right now. But anyway, we got there on a Sunday evening. This is about 7 o'clock. And the concert started at 8. And they had torches lit with, they had candles. They had these torches that looked like bulrushes, what we call them here. And so I was, they had so many of those torches. I took one of the torches with a candle, and the candles, grease got all over my overcoat. And those people went from the station. And they all walked in the middle street from the station to this hall, which was about four or five squares. And they had a jazz club there, and they made all of us honorary members of this jazz club. We all got, they gave us all pins. They gave George bouquets. And the people welcomed George Lewis so well. I mean, they gave him such a ovation, till he had to cry. He broke out of tears in this, in these places. And they all were fine. And this jazz, we went to another place. We played at the jazz club. Had a dinner for the band after the concert. And they all were young kids. They arranged, I say, from about 12 years old to about 24. All young, all young kids. And we all ate dinner. And from there we played one or two pieces. We had to leave, we had to get a train out and go back to Denmark. Then we were made honorary members of a club in England. And we played everywhere in England, I think that a band could go and play it. Because we, I don't know, we played so many places there. And everywhere we played at though, we had, we had tremendous crowds. And I think we played six concert in London. And all of those were really good crowds at all of the concert. And it was excellent because we didn't have a bad concert. And then playing behind Louis Armstrong within a week, a week or five days. And then Count Basie was playing three or four days behind us. So we was right in the middle of those two bands. But all the concerts was really good.
But your band went over better than any of them.

Well, everybody said that they thought that the band, we know that we had bigger crowds in Louis and many places. And everybody liked the band. They thought the band was better than Louis' band. They claimed that Louis made some changes in his band. Well, they played better together.
I mean, he's a big star, but sometimes his band isn't the greatest.
